dharana.numbering_edition: Jaideva Singh 1979 (dhāraṇā 1 = verse 24; dhāraṇā 82 = verses 105–106 and dhāraṇā 89 = verses 113–114, otherwise one verse each; dhāraṇā 112 = verse 137)
dharana.sanskrit_iast: pīnāṃ ca durbalāṃ śaktiṃ dhyātvā dvādaśagocare | praviśya hṛdaye dhyāyan muktaḥ svātantryam āpnuyāt ||
dharana.sanskrit_source: GRETIL e-text, compared with Wallis's concordance, Pradīpaka and the Singh scan
sanskrit_variants: verse 55: GRETIL reads pināṃ; corrected to pīnāṃ ('thick') with Wallis and Pradīpaka. Last quarter: GRETIL, Singh and Pradīpaka read muktaḥ svātantryam āpnuyāt. Singh's notes record that Abhinavagupta (Tantrāloka 15.480–81) reads suptaḥ svācchandyam āpnuyāt and Kṣemarāja (Spandanirṇaya) reads svapnasvātantryam āpnuyāt; Wallis prints 'svapna- (or muktaḥ)'.
dharana.rendering: Having meditated on the breath-power as thick and as thin in the region of the dvādaśānta, and entering the heart while meditating, one becomes free and gains sovereign freedom. (In the reading of Abhinavagupta and Kṣemarāja: one gains freedom in dream.)
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh translates: gross prāṇaśakti made frail and subtle by yogic discipline (particularly prāṇāyāma) and meditated on in the dvādaśānta or the heart. He then gives Swami Lakshmanjoo's traditional reading: 'thick' means breathing in and out audibly, 'thin' means slowly; meditating so at the dvādaśānta and the heart while falling asleep, one gains freedom in dreams. Singh records that Abhinavagupta (Tantrāloka 15) reads suptaḥ svācchandyam āpnuyāt and Kṣemarāja (Spandanirṇaya) svapnasvātantryam āpnuyāt. Wallis: prāṇa thick in the heart, tenuous at the dvādaśānta, and 'freedom in one's dreams'.
dharana.technique_name: Thick Breath, Thin Breath, Entering the Heart
dharana.instruction: Breathe a few soft audible breaths, let the breath grow thin, and rest attention in the heart.

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 55: Freedom in the dream state (Y28 ~ A3)

source_disagreements: Last quarter: GRETIL, Singh and Pradīpaka read muktaḥ svātantryam ('freed, gains sovereignty'); Abhinavagupta reads suptaḥ svācchandyam and Kṣemarāja svapnasvātantryam ('freedom in dream'); Wallis prints both.

Which place is 'thick' and which 'thin': Singh reads gross breath made subtle, meditated in the dvādaśānta or the heart; Wallis reads thick in the heart and thin at the dvādaśānta; Lakshmanjoo (via Singh) reads 'audible' and 'slow'.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position. In Lakshmanjoo's reading the practice is done while falling asleep, so lying down is natural.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 55 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

points: the dvādaśānta (commentarial: in front of the nose or above the head)
geometry.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the breath travelling between two places, the dvādaśānta and the heart, sometimes full and audible, sometimes thin and slow.
geometry.svg_hint: a breath line between a point in front of the face and a point in the chest, drawn thick then thin
geometry.honesty: Geometry records the dharana's own map of attention, not a body shape. Locations marked 'commentarial' come from commentary, not from the verse.

reaction.name: Coarse to fine
reaction.summary: School metaphor only: a coarse, audible breath is allowed to become thin and slow, and attention enters the heart with it. Not a biochemical or medical claim.

breath.lands_in: the heart, as the breath becomes thin
breath.cue: A few soft, audible breaths, then let the breath become thin and slow on its own. Never strain or hold. Natural breath is always fine.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

orientation.cue: Begin with the breath at the dvādaśānta, then let attention enter the heart
orientation.gravity: Let the floor or chair carry the body completely; there is no posture to hold
orientation.gaze: Eyes closed; this can be done lying down before sleep
orientation.degrees_hint: No angle target: the VBT gives no posture for this dharana

attention.primary: The breath-power at the dvādaśānta and in the heart, first coarse, then fine
attention.secondary: Entering the heart as the breath thins

adiyogi.verse_paraphrase: Having meditated on the breath-power as thick and as thin in the region of the dvādaśānta, and entering the heart while meditating, one becomes free and gains sovereign freedom. (In the reading of Abhinavagupta and Kṣemarāja: one gains freedom in dream.)
adiyogi.method_summary: Breathe a few soft, audible breaths with attention at the dvādaśānta. Let the breath become thin and slow by itself. Then let attention enter the heart and rest there; in the traditional reading, while falling asleep. No breath-holding and no forceful breathing.

honesty.disclosure: Door 032 follows Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 32 (verse 55) in Jaideva Singh's numbering. The door-to-dharana index is a School of 112 Doorways teaching device. Singh's sequence is one edition's count, not an ancient one-to-one canon. The seat, counts, reaction and beat scripts are school additions.
honesty.notes: pairing_type is school_device: the dharana is the content, while the door index, seat and pacing are the school's.
flags: Door index = Jaideva Singh dharana number: Door 032 is dharana 32, verse 55. Other editions number differently (see dharana.numbering_variants).

The English is a school paraphrase, not a quotation from any translator.

safety.pain_rule: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.
safety.open_seat_alternate: This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.
safety.contraindication_notes: General practice caution only; not medical advice. Do not force the breath or hold it; Singh's mention of breath-control is not taught here. Stop if light-headed. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.

beats.title: Name the door
beats.script: This is Door 032: thick breath, thin breath, entering the heart. Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 32, verse 55.

beats.title: Geometry
beats.script: No shape to make. Sit, or lie down as if for sleep. The map is the breath between the dvādaśānta and the heart.

beats.title: Orientation
beats.script: Let the floor or the chair carry you. Eyes closed or soft.

beats.title: Breath
beats.script: A few soft, audible breaths, then let them grow thin and slow by themselves. No forcing, no hold.

beats.title: Attention
beats.script: Let the thinning breath carry attention into the heart. Rest there. If you are lying down, you may let sleep come.

beats.title: Reaction cue
beats.script: School image: a coarse breath becoming fine. A metaphor, not medicine.

beats.title: Adiyogi thread
beats.script: Verse 55: meditate on the breath-power as thick and thin at the dvādaśānta, enter the heart, and one gains freedom, in one reading freedom in dream. Never strain the breath.

beats.title: Exit / integrate
beats.script: Let the practice go. Take one free breath. Open the eyes and look around the room.
